findings: The refresh-in-progress branch (`await sleep(50); return currentToken;`) does not actually wait for the in-flight refresh to finish — it waits a fixed 50ms and then returns whatever `currentToken` currently holds, without re-checking `refreshing` or the token's validity. If the real `/auth/refresh` round trip takes longer than 50ms (entirely normal under network latency/congestion), waiting callers return the OLD token value before `currentToken = newToken` has run. Since the docstring states the server invalidates `oldToken` the instant it receives the refresh request, that returned token is already dead server-side, so the caller's subsequent authenticated request gets a 401 — this is exactly the 'intermittent logout with no clear repro' symptom, since it only triggers when refresh latency happens to exceed the hardcoded 50ms window.

`refreshToken()` is awaited with no try/catch/finally in `getToken()`. If `api.post('/auth/refresh', ...)` ever rejects (timeout, 5xx, transient network blip), the exception propagates out of `getToken()` but the line `refreshing = false` is never reached, so `refreshing` is left permanently `true`. From that moment on, every future call to `getToken()` for the lifetime of the module skips the refresh branch entirely (since `!refreshing` is now always false), falls into the 50ms-sleep-then-return-`currentToken` branch, and can never trigger a real refresh again — a single transient failure permanently disables authentication until a full page reload, which is a much larger-blast-radius version of the same 'random logout' report.

Because `currentToken` is module-initialized to `null`, the same fixed-50ms-wait defect (finding 1) has a worse special case at cold start / first load: if multiple `getToken()` calls fire concurrently before the very first refresh completes (e.g. several components mounting at once), the callers that lose the refresh race and whose 50ms sleep elapses before the first refresh resolves will return `null` (not merely a stale token) from `return currentToken;`. That null/undefined value then gets used as the auth token for a request, guaranteeing an unauthenticated failure rather than just a possibly-stale one — a distinct, more severe failure mode from the same underlying synchronization gap.
